content.text: Whole-cell selection can preserve every DG coefficient exactly. The other cases worth covering are contiguous ranges, negative indices, and component selection—`comp=1` must select the entire coefficient block for field 1. I’ll also define boundary behavior: floats outside the domain snap to an end cell, ties choose the lower-index cell, and empty selections are rejected.

content.text:
The new quadratic tests exposed a bug in the existing projection path: projecting multiple fields together produces incorrect output and can corrupt memory. I’m using the native-bridge skill to fix this by projecting each field separately, as the other DG operations already do.

When every dimension is selected, I’m following the existing native convention: return the evaluated value as a constant DG field on a dummy `[0, 1]` cell, since Gkeyll has no zero-dimensional basis.

content.text:
Implemented the clarified behavior:

- Scalar indices and floats evaluate at the selected cell center and remove that dimension.
- Floats snap to the nearest center.
- Ranges retain whole cells; negative indices and complete-field component selection work.

Selecting every dimension returns a constant DG field on a dummy `[0, 1]` cell.

Limitation: scalar selection requires native projection support; unsupported basis/orders, including p0, raise `NotImplementedError`.

Full suite checked; corrected checks passed on rerun. Six tests skipped.
Why does selecting scalars require projection support? Shouldn't it just collapse to a certain dimension along that index? So like, select all the points where --z1 has index 5

Yes—`--z1 5` should select cell index 5 along that axis, keeping all cells along the other axes.

For raw DG data, each cell contains polynomial coefficients rather than point samples. To also **remove `z1`**, as you requested, we evaluate that polynomial’s `z1` dependence at the selected cell’s center. The remaining coefficients describe a lower-dimensional polynomial.

That’s a **restriction of the polynomial**, and it can be computed directly from the basis. It doesn’t fundamentally require interpolation or native projection kernels. A plain array squeeze would leave coefficients associated with the original, higher-dimensional basis.

My implementation unnecessarily tied this to Gkeyll’s projection-kernel coverage. In particular, excluding p0 was unjustified: a constant polynomial can be restricted directly.

There might be a misunderstanding. So say we load a 6 coefficient 3D array. Then the data is like (c0,c1,c2,c3,c4,c5,c6) on coodrinates (x,y,z). Select should select, for instance, y=0.5. So we are looking at a grid (x,y=0.5,z). This select operation should snap to the data which is closest to 0.5, colapsing that dimension. This doesn't require any interpolation. Similarly, selecting index 5 in the y direction should not require interpolation. Is that how this is implemented. Is there a misunderstanding? I don't see why we need the eval_at_coord_proj operator here

There was a misunderstanding. **You want to slice the coefficient array, preserving every coefficient unchanged.** The current implementation instead evaluates the polynomial using `eval_at_coord_proj`, so it does more than you intended.

Your operation is:

```python
# values.shape == (nx, ny, nz, ncoeff)
j = nearest_cell_center(y, 0.5)  # or j = 5
selected = values[:, j, :, :]
# selected.shape == (nx, nz, ncoeff)
```

That requires neither interpolation nor polynomial evaluation. The selected grid records the fixed coordinate `y[j]`, and all coefficient vectors are copied unchanged.

The distinction matters for metadata: those vectors still contain coefficients of the original **3D basis**, even though the selected array has only two varying spatial axes. We must preserve that basis information and the fixed cell’s location; treating those coefficients as a 2D basis would be incorrect.

I interpreted “collapse the dimension” as reducing the polynomial’s dimension. You meant collapsing the **array’s cell-index dimension**. For that behavior, `eval_at_coord_proj` should not be used.
